title: How the New End Date of a Long-Term Hardship Hold Extension Is Set
content:
**Portal help — Hardship and Protective Holds.** When a consumer extends a running Long-Term Hardship Hold, the number of days the extension adds sets the new end date. That number is defined as follows.

The days the long-term extension adds are the tier's extension days, counted from the day after the hold's current end date, so that the new end date is the current end date plus the days added. The days the long-term extension adds are a whole number of calendar days and are not rounded.

## What goes into the figure

| Item | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| The tier's extension days | The extension days of the Long-Term Hardship Hold in the product's schedule of hold lengths and extensions |
| The hold's current end date | The end date shown on the hold's record |
| New end date | The current end date plus the days the long-term extension adds |

## Worked example (hypothetical)

A Long-Term Hardship Hold has a current end date of 31 August. Taking, for the illustration, an extension-days figure of 90 calendar days:

1. The extension is counted from the day after the current end date, 1 September.
2. The days the long-term extension adds: 90, a whole number with no rounding.
3. New end date: 31 August plus 90 days, that is 29 November. The days 1 September through 29 November number 90.

## Questions answered

**Does the extension start on the current end date or the day after?** It is counted from the day after the current end date; the current end date itself is already covered.

**Is a part day ever added?** No. The figure is a whole number of calendar days and is not rounded.
